bib.title: Skills as Verifiable Artifacts: A Trust Schema and a Biconditional Correctness Criterion for Human-in-the-Loop Agent Runtimes

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Skills as Verifiable Artifacts: A Trust Schema and a Biconditional Correctness Criterion for Human-in-the-Loop Agent Runtimes", Alfredo Metere (Enclawed, LLC, California; sole author). arXiv 2605.00424v2 [cs.CR], preprint, dated 18 May 2026 (arXiv stamp 15 May). No venue.

COVERAGE: 17 of 17 pages, 50,972 chars. I read every section, Table 2 and the reference list. The extraction was clean. I did not run the figure tool; the text shows no figures, only Tables 1 and 2.

CORE CLAIM
A skill (SKILL.md plus scripts) is untrusted code until it is verified. A signature or clearance check does not make it trusted. If every irreversible call needs human approval (HITL), operators rubber-stamp. The paper therefore adds a separate verification step with four fixed levels: `unverified` (default), `declared`, `tested` and `formal`. The HITL gate depends on that level. A single check, called the biconditional, compares what the world shows with what the audit log says was approved and executed. The source is mostly a position and design paper with a small mechanical test. The schema and guidelines G1–G12 come from the author's own framework, enclawed, which is cited as [17].

HEADLINE NUMBERS (empirical, §6.1)
1. Sweep. This tests the check itself, not any model's safety.
   - Setup: N∈{10,50,200} files, K∈{2,4,8} agents, R∈{5,10,25} rounds, 200 seeds per cell. Faults F1–F4 were injected deterministically at round R/2. The broker approves everything.
   - Result: zero false positives and zero false negatives.
   - Quote: "Across 27 × 200× 5 = 27,000 runs the biconditional gave zero false positives (FPs) on clean runs and zero false negatives (FNs) on injected faults: Wilson 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.999, 1.000]" (p11)
   - Caveat: the faults were injected by the author's own driver, so this is close to a tautology. The paper itself says the result "empirically matches the formal claim of Proposition 1".
2. Cross-model run.
   - Setup: ten LLM families acting as adversaries (one Gemini, three Groq, five Ollama, one OpenRouter), over Discord and Telegram backends. Three subjects were tested: an unhardened passthrough, the OSS runtime (biconditional, audit and a data-loss-prevention scanner), and the full deployment (adds a behavioral monitor).
   - Result: "Across 9,724 mediated payloads (4,816 adversarial, 4,908 legit), the upstream passthrough blocked 0.0% (CI [0.000, 0.001]); the OSS runtime achieved 76.3% recall (CI [0.751, 0.775]) at 0.0% false-positive rate (FPR); the full deployment achieved 80.2% recall (CI [0.791, 0.813]) at 0.6% FPR." (p12)
   - The author says recall is 1.000 on the subset where the adversary actually produced a fault-shaped payload. The paper reports that figure but gives no count of that subset.
3. No ablation. There is no comparison of verification levels, no test of G1–G12 components, and no measurement of rubber-stamping or HITL load. The central claim that verification makes HITL sustainable is asserted, not measured.

DESIGN ELEMENTS WORTH KEEPING
- Fixed enum of verification levels, not a score: "A continuous 'trust score' would allow the agent to argue itself into permission gradients" (p5).
- The agent cannot edit a loaded skill. Any attempt is treated as an irreversible call, goes through HITL, and is logged with before and after hashes (§3.2, G12).
- Verification is set at bootstrap only and never raised during a session.
- Reversible calls go through a transaction buffer. Irreversible calls (email, publish, on-chain, remote delete) go through request, decide, execute and audit.
- Reversibility is decided by which dispatch path a call took, not by inspecting syscalls.
- Broker types: deny-all, policy (a file the LLM cannot reach), interactive (default deny on timeout), webhook.
- G10, no bypass switch: no flag or override may disable the gate or the audit log.
- G2, deny-by-default at every boundary.
- Eight attack families for a CI pen-test corpus (G8).

QUOTES
- "a skill is untrusted code until it is verified, and the runtime that loads it must enforce that default rather than infer trust from a signature, a clearance, or a registry of origin" (abstract, p1; the extraction runs "code" and "until" together).
- "This is operationally untenable: operators under load rubber-stamp every prompt, degrading the gate into a fiction." (p2)
- "It is not a value-level correctness criterion" (paraphrased from p9; the exact text reads "It isnot a value-level correctness criterion"). Prefer this one: "The criterion is necessary, not sufficient, for full safety" (p10).
- "The runtime must not expose a build flag, environment variable, runtime API, or operator override that disables the HITL gate..." (G10, p13). The extraction renders it as "must notexpose".

LIMITS
- The paper concedes five failures the check misses (§5.4):
  - F5, wrong content written to an approved target.
  - Read-only exfiltration through a covert channel.
  - Time-of-check/time-of-use races.
  - An attacker acting on the same target as a legitimate approval.
  - The check works only on (operation, target), not on the payload.
- It tests only deletion and edit of small files. It tests no real skill from a registry and no human operators.
- The `formal` level is "aspirational".
- Out of scope: a compromised signing key or runtime binary, hardware trust anchors, and model-weight attacks.
- Open problems it names: label declassification, signer revocation mid-session, and hardware-rooted trust.
- A vendor author evaluates his own framework. Artifacts are said to be released but I did not check them.
- It cites a concurrent survey [27] claiming about 26% of community skills carry a vulnerability. That figure is secondhand and I did not read the survey.

BUILDS ON
- Bell–LaPadula 1976.
- The object-capability tradition: Miller 2003 and 2006.
- Hash-chained audit logs: Schneier and Kelsey 1999.
- SELinux (Loscocco and Smalley 2001), Asbestos (2005) and HiStar (2006).
- Thompson 1984, "Reflections on Trusting Trust".
- Complements AgentSpec (Wang et al. 2025), Doshi et al. 2026 (ICSE NIER), SafeAgent (2026), SkillProbe (2026) and Xu and Yan 2026 (arXiv 2602.12430).

NOTE PLACEMENT
- Best fit is 04-execution-boundaries.md. It matches the sections on permission gates, "a role label is not a sandbox" (a signature or clearance is not trust) and "encode constraints, don't document them" (G10, G2 and a policy file the LLM cannot reach). It also supports hooks and trust zones through the reversible/irreversible split and the broker.
- A secondary pointer, one sentence at most, belongs in the 03-tool-design.md section "MCP supply-chain risks" (registry attacker, untrusted by default) and "Writing a skill" (declare the capabilities a skill needs; skills are immutable at runtime). The core is runtime enforcement, so the main citation goes in note 04.
- Treat it as a design proposal, not as evidence. The 76.3% figure is the only number worth citing, and only with its setup. It is the OSS runtime's recall against LLM-generated adversarial payloads in the author's own harness.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: none. The paper has no figures. Table 1 (capability vocabulary, p6) is the closest thing to a candidate.

PROBLEMS: none. The text contains no embedded instructions. The extraction merges some words ("untrusted codeuntil", "isnot"). I wrote the page-text to /tmp/metere.txt.
